opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of that pessimism comes from experience with negotiations where the two sides see the issue as fundamentally zero-sum, or where one side suspects the other is only at the table to buy time. Think of trade disputes, Taiwan, or the South China Sea. There, what one side gains the other tends to lose, and each side's domestic politics rewards toughness. Diplomats who've spent decades in that environment understandably come to expect very little.

Superintelligence could be different in a few important ways. The first is that the core risk isn't primarily that the other side wins. It's that nobody wins. If you build a system far more capable than any human and you can't reliably control it, it doesn't matter much whether it was built in Beijing or San Francisco. That makes it look much more like a shared-threat problem than a rivalry problem. The closest analogies are things like nuclear arms control in the later Cold War, or the Montreal Protocol on ozone. In those cases, adversaries with deep mutual distrust still managed to reach real agreements, because both came to see that the alternative was bad for them too.

The second point is that we have some evidence the Chinese leadership takes these risks seriously. Chinese officials, scientists and AI researchers have spoken about catastrophic and loss-of-control risks, and Chinese experts have taken part in international dialogues on AI safety alongside Western scientists. That doesn't guarantee anything, but it isn't a situation where one side simply dismisses the danger.

Third, a lot of the diplomatic pessimism is about verification and trust. Those are real problems, but advanced AI development has some features that may make verification more tractable than people assume. It depends on enormous concentrations of specialised chips, huge data centres and large amounts of energy. Those are physical, hard-to-hide inputs, and the supply chain runs through a small number of chokepoints. That gives you handles for monitoring that you don't have for, say, cyberweapons.

Finally, I'd say we shouldn't treat past failures as a law of nature. Diplomats are often pessimistic right up until the moment the political conditions change, and then agreements that seemed impossible come together quite quickly. If it becomes widely understood among leaders on both sides that an uncontrolled race toward superintelligence threatens everyone, including the regimes themselves, the incentives shift. Our job now is partly to prepare the groundwork, so that the ideas, institutions and technical verification tools are ready when that political window opens.

r001.rationale: The response argues that uncontrollable superintelligence could threaten everyone, including both regimes, shifting incentives toward agreement and overcoming diplomats’ pessimism.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the pessimism is understandable. People who've spent their careers in these negotiations have watched a lot of them fail, and they've seen how hard it is to get agreement even on things where the interests look fairly aligned. So I don't want to wave that away.

But I think there are a few reasons to think superintelligence is a somewhat different case from, say, trade or human rights or the South China Sea.

The first is that this is a situation where the leading powers face a genuinely shared threat. In most negotiations, one side's gain is roughly the other side's loss, and you're haggling over where the line falls. But if you really take seriously the possibility that a race to build superintelligence could end with nobody in control of the outcome, then both the United States and China have a very strong interest in not ending up there. That's closer to the structure of the nuclear arms control agreements than it is to a trade dispute. And we did manage to get some of those, even at the height of the Cold War, between adversaries who trusted each other far less than the US and China do today.

The second thing is that the Chinese leadership has, in its own statements, expressed real concern about losing control of this technology. There's a tendency in the West to assume China just wants to win the race and will do whatever it takes. But the evidence I've seen suggests the Party is quite worried about systems it can't control, partly for reasons of its own political stability. So the concern isn't purely a Western one that we'd have to talk them into. It may already be partly there.

The third point is that the alternative to negotiating is to race, and I think if you put the racing scenario in front of people clearly, it looks very bad for everyone. If the leading lab in one country gets to superintelligence first and it goes well for them, the other country faces a situation that's potentially existential from its point of view. If it goes badly, it's bad for everyone. So the pessimism about diplomacy needs to be weighed against the pessimism we should have about the alternative. It's not that negotiation is easy. It's that the thing you're comparing it to is also extremely hard and arguably much more dangerous.

And then the last thing I'd say is that we don't need a grand comprehensive treaty tomorrow. A lot of what made Cold War arms control possible was starting small, with confidence-building measures, hotlines, verification experiments, scientist-to-scientist dialogue, and building up from there. There's quite a lot of that kind of groundwork that could happen now, well before any formal agreement, and it doesn't require either side to trust the other very much. It just requires both sides to recognise that they'd rather know what's going on than not.

So I'm not saying it's likely to succeed. I'm saying the pessimism is calibrated on cases that have a different structure, and that when the stakes are this high, even a modest chance of success is worth taking very seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says superintelligence poses a shared, potentially existential threat, making the racing alternative extremely dangerous for both countries. It concludes that even a modest chance of negotiation success is worth taking seriously despite diplomats’ pessimism.

astra-6.text:
I think that pessimism may be quite reasonable as a judgment about the negotiations diplomats are involved in today. But we should be cautious about extrapolating it to a situation where both sides believe that their survival could be at stake.

If the US and China both came to think that developing superintelligence carried a substantial risk of losing control, then there would be a very strong shared interest in avoiding that outcome. You might distrust the other government profoundly while still believing that it doesn’t want to lose control of its own future. That gives you something to negotiate around.

Of course, it wouldn’t make verification easy, or eliminate the fear that the other side might gain an advantage. But it could change what both sides were willing to accept to resolve those problems. So I wouldn’t say that agreement is inevitable. I’d say that the prospects for agreement depend on how the parties understand the stakes, and those could be very different from the stakes in negotiations today.

r001.rationale: The response argues that if both sides see superintelligence as a threat to their survival and control of their future, their shared interest could make agreement more possible than in today’s negotiations, despite diplomats’ current pessimism.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think their pessimism is worth taking seriously. They have experience of how difficult these negotiations can be. But we should ask how closely that experience applies to this particular problem.

Most negotiations with China involve substantial conflicts of interest. With superintelligence, there’s potentially a very large shared interest: neither government wants to lose control of the future to systems that it can’t control. Even if you care primarily about your own country’s power and security, that’s a reason to want an agreement.

That doesn’t make agreement easy. There are still questions about trust, verification, and whether each side thinks it could get ahead. But it could change the negotiating situation quite substantially. You might both prefer to slow down, provided you can be confident that the other side is slowing down too.

So I wouldn’t take pessimism about negotiations in other areas as settling this question. We need to explore whether that shared interest can support a verifiable agreement. The stakes are sufficiently high that it seems very important to try.

r001.rationale: The response says shared interests could make agreement more plausible and that high stakes make trying important. It does not argue that the high stakes could overcome diplomats’ pessimism; it says that pessimism does not settle the question.
